title: Liturgy (CCC 1066–1070)
hook: liturgy means the work of the people, now the work of God among us

segments.voice: Yesterday, amen: the Creed's last word, and in the Apocalypse a name for Christ. Your line was so be it. When did you slow down and mean a yes? Today, the second part of the Catechism begins. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

Stand at the back of a Catholic church during Mass and just listen. The priest says a line, and the whole room answers him. He prays, and the room says amen. People stand, sit, kneel, sing, walk forward, go quiet, all together, with hardly anyone giving directions out loud. To a visitor it can look like a show with an audience that happens to know the script. The Catechism paints a different picture, one with no audience in it at all. The first part of the Catechism was about what Catholics believe. The second part is about how they celebrate it, and it opens with one word.
screen: `THE ROOM ANSWERS.` → `NOBODY GIVES DIRECTIONS.` → `NOT A SHOW.`

segments.voice: The word is liturgy. First, where it comes from. The Catechism explains that the word originally meant a public work, a service done in the name of the people, or on their behalf. Not a private hobby. Something done for everyone. Second, what the Church did with it. In Christian use, the Catechism says, liturgy means the people of God taking part in the work of God. And the work of God here is big: through the liturgy, Catholics believe, Christ himself keeps carrying on the work of saving the world, in his Church, with his Church, and through his Church. So the people's work and God's work end up being the same work, done together. Third, it's wider than one room. The Catechism notices that the New Testament uses this word for more than worship. It's used for Zechariah serving in the Temple, in Luke's Gospel. It's used for preaching the Gospel. And it's used for practical help, like the care one church sent to Paul through a messenger. Worship, preaching, charity: all of it, liturgy. Fourth, the people have a part. The Second Vatican Council asked for the faithful to take part fully, consciously and actively. That's one reason the room answers. When the priest says the Lord be with you, the reply isn't politeness. It's the people doing their part of the work. So the next time a Mass looks like a show, remember the Catechism's picture: there's no audience. Everyone in the room has a job.
screen: `A PUBLIC WORK.` · `THE PEOPLE IN THE WORK OF GOD.` · `WORSHIP, PREACHING, CHARITY.` · `NO AUDIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take part fully once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next time you'll be in a shared moment: a Mass, a service, a family meal, a meeting, a birthday song. Decide now on one way you'll take part in it fully instead of watching. Answer out loud, not under your breath. Sing instead of mouthing. Put the phone away. Listen to the reading as if it were addressed to you. Hold that one choice in mind. If you pray, you can offer it ahead of time. If you don't, simply plan to show up all the way. The bell holds the time.
Liturgy. Once a public work done for the people. For Catholics, the people of God taking part in the work of God, with no one in the room just watching. Today's word.
Your line: the people's work. Today, wherever you're part of something shared, do your part out loud: the answer, the song, the help. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

howItsDone: At Mass Catholics take part through spoken responses, singing, standing, sitting and kneeling together, and in roles such as reader, server, cantor and minister of Communion.

fork.setup: you're at Mass for the first time. the priest says, the Lord be with you. what is the room doing?
options: answering, because the people have a part in the work
waiting for the music to start
fork.reveal: the room answers him. the Catechism calls liturgy the people of God taking part in the work of God: there's no audience.

original.note: Greek: a public work or service. The Catechism says it came to mean the people's share in the work of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: the order of service printed in a booklet.
what it means: the people of God taking part in the work of God, with no one in the room just watching.
what a scholar hears: once a public work done for the people; the New Testament uses it for Temple service, preaching and charity.

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy

notes: CCC paraphrased (1069 original meaning 'public work' / service in the name of or on behalf of the people; the people of God's participation in the work of God; Christ continues the work of redemption in, with and through his Church; 1070 New Testament uses for divine worship, proclamation of the Gospel and active charity, citing Luke 1:23, Romans 15:16, Philippians 2:14–17, 25, 30, and others). The etymology is taken from CCC 1069. Confirm.
'The care one church sent to Paul through a messenger' refers to Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:25, 30). Confirm the CCC cites it this way.
Sacrosanctum Concilium 14 ('full, conscious, and active participation') is paraphrased, since the Vatican's English is copyrighted.
'The Lord be with you' is the priest's greeting at Mass; the people's response is not quoted (current English translation is copyrighted).
Start of Part Two (How we celebrate).
